entries.clue: Maybe a piece in the Guardian (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half is not a synonym but an instance: the word 'a' is one of these, and 'maybe' is the setter's licence for offering an example instead of a meaning.

blocks.note: read as journalism — a newspaper's pages are made of these, and the paper named is the one this puzzle ran in
read as grammar — 'a' is one of the two little words English puts in front of a noun, and 'maybe' says it is an example

annotation.surface: A piece of writing that may have appeared in the Guardian.
annotation.walkthrough: The smallest word in the clue is the one doing the work: 'a' is not part of the phrase but an instance of the thing. The paper named is the paper the puzzle ran in.
annotation.definitionFit: An article is a piece of writing in a newspaper, and 'a' is the indefinite article, so both halves land on the same seven letters.

entries.clue: With difficulty, cheers up, a hot drink having been knocked over (2,1,4)

indicatorNotes.up: This is a down answer, so anything going up is read from the bottom, and the letters beside it arrive back to front.
indicatorNotes.having been knocked over: Something knocked over is lying the other way round, so those letters are read from the far end.

blocks.note: ta is the everyday British thank-you, and 'cheers' is the same word of thanks; turned round it reads AT
the single letter is the word itself
h = hot and to sup is to drink, and HSUP turned round reads PUSH

annotation.surface: Somebody being cheered up until a hot drink goes over.
annotation.walkthrough: Both instructions here are turnarounds, and a down answer is what lets 'up' be one of them. 'Cheers' is the British thank-you, not a toast and not the cheering the word after it suggests.
annotation.definitionFit: 'At a push' is what the English say when a thing can only just be managed — you could do it, with difficulty and no margin.

entries.clue: Awfully abhorrent men not naturally suited to something (2,3,6,4)

indicatorNotes.Awfully: Awfully means badly, and letters badly set out are letters no longer in the order they were given.

blocks.note: fifteen letters for the jumble, the full width of the grid

annotation.surface: Dreadful men who were never cut out for the job.
annotation.walkthrough: Hamlet gives the phrase, and the fodder settles its spelling: the sitcom 'To the Manor Born' was a pun on it, and these letters carry the three Ns that the other spelling wants.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone to the manner born took to a way of life as though born for it, which is exactly being naturally suited to it.

entries.clue: Clubs give in to spreading of knowledge acquisition (9)

indicatorNotes.spreading: What spreads goes out in every direction at once, so the letters before it need not stay in the order they were given.

blocks.note: c = clubs, the card suit on a scoresheet
eight letters re-set to follow the card suit

annotation.surface: Clubs surrendering to the spread of learning.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Clubs' is the card suit's single letter, not a group of people or a set of weapons. The definition is an adjective, which the 'of' standing in front of it quietly tells you.
annotation.definitionFit: Cognitive means having to do with knowing — perception, memory, learning — so it is the adjective for anything concerning how knowledge is picked up.

entries.clue: Force through former law (5)

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, and ex- is the prefix for anything former
an act is a single law as parliament passes it

annotation.surface: Pushing a piece of old legislation through.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is a bill being shoved through parliament, so 'law' looks like the whole body of it and is one single statute instead. The definition is a verb, not an adjective about precision.
annotation.definitionFit: To exact something — a fine, a promise, revenge — is to force it out of someone who would rather not hand it over.

entries.clue: Big town mostly protected by historic royal account (7)

indicatorNotes.mostly: Mostly means very nearly all, so the word beside it hands over everything except its final letter.
indicatorNotes.protected by: Whatever protects a thing closes round it, so the word that follows splits and stands on either side of the letters before it.

blocks.note: real is an old adjective meaning royal, the sense still standing in Spanish names like Real Madrid
a city is a big town, and all but its last letter is wanted

annotation.surface: A town kept safe by some ancient royal record.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Real' is an old adjective meaning royal, which is the job 'historic' is doing — warning that the word is out of date rather than describing the king. The definition is the narration sense.
annotation.definitionFit: A recital is a detailed account of events — a recital of her grievances — the same word as the one for a solo concert.

entries.clue: Tries to block genuine practice run (9)

indicatorNotes.to block: Something that blocks a thing stands in the middle of it, so the letters named first are planted inside the word that follows.

blocks.note: real = genuine, and the four letters part to take the rest between them
a judge who tries a case hears it, which is the court's own word for the job

annotation.surface: Attempts to obstruct a genuine practice run.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Tries' is the courtroom verb — a judge who tries a case hears it — rather than an attempt. The four letters for 'genuine' wrap HEARS, and 5 across wraps its city in the same four.
annotation.definitionFit: A rehearsal is the run-through a cast or an orchestra does before the performance, so it is practice for the real event.

entries.clue: Pronunciation of ‘betrays’ in Chambers (5)

indicatorNotes.Pronunciation of: A pronunciation is what a word sounds like rather than how it is spelt, so the answer only has to match the sound.

blocks.note: to sell someone is to betray them — he sold his friends to the police — and that same sound is spelt another way

annotation.surface: How the dictionary says a word for betrayal is pronounced.
annotation.walkthrough: Chambers in italics is the dictionary, and that is where the surface keeps you. The definition wants the ordinary sense of chambers: the bare little rooms of a prison or a monastery.
annotation.definitionFit: A cell is the plainest sort of chamber, the bare room a monk or a prisoner is shut into, so the plurals mean the same.

entries.clue: Robust firm, American, made acceptable car components (5,2,3,5)

blocks.note: firm meat is tough meat, the adjective rather than the company
A is the standard abbreviation for American
once you have sold an idea to somebody you have made it acceptable to them
a car's boot is its luggage compartment in British usage, so every car has one

annotation.surface: A sturdy American firm that got its car parts approved.
annotation.walkthrough: The pieces do not fall where the printed spaces do: A and SOLD join a letter to the left of the printed AS OLD. 'Firm' is the adjective, not the company the comma sets up.
annotation.definitionFit: 'Tough as old boots' is the standard English comparison for anything robust, from cheap meat to an unkillable relative — leather that has outlasted years of wear.

entries.clue: African kingdom’s extremely large lush house (7)

indicatorNotes.extremely: The extremes of a word are its two ends, so only the first and last letters of the word beside it are taken.

blocks.note: the two extreme letters of LARGE, first and last
a lush is a habitual drinker, and a sot is the older word for one
ho is the estate agent's and the atlas's short form of house

annotation.surface: A very large leafy house belonging to an African kingdom.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lush' is the drinker rather than the greenery the surface wants, and 'extremely' is an instruction rather than a remark about the size. The kingdom itself is ringed by South Africa on every side.
annotation.definitionFit: Lesotho is the mountain kingdom of southern Africa, landlocked inside South Africa and ruled by a king of its own.

entries.clue: Deplorably, a pro laughs at pinching Tramp’s memorabilia collections (9,6)

indicatorNotes.Deplorably: Something done deplorably is done badly, and letters badly arranged are letters taken in any order at all.
indicatorNotes.pinching: To pinch a thing is to grip it, so the jumbled letters close round the three named and hold them whole inside.

blocks.note: twelve letters, jumbled, then parted before the last to take the tramp
a bum is a tramp, the American word for a vagrant; its three letters go in unchanged

annotation.surface: A professional laughing at the theft of a tramp's possessions.
annotation.walkthrough: Tramp is capitalised to look like somebody's name, and what is wanted is the American word for a vagrant. Fifteen letters is a long jumble, and the three that sit intact inside it are the easiest to miss.
annotation.definitionFit: Autograph albums are the books fans fill with signatures got in person, so they are collections of memorabilia gathered one page at a time.

entries.clue: Partly cauterised organs (5)

indicatorNotes.Partly: Only part of the word beside it is wanted, and that part is a run of its letters taken exactly as they stand.

blocks.note: the five letters sit unbroken in the middle of caUTERIsed

annotation.surface: Organs that have been partly cauterised.
annotation.walkthrough: A surgical surface is the best hiding place for a surgical answer: nothing in the sentence looks out of place, and 'partly' is the only signal that anything is buried.
annotation.definitionFit: Uteri is the Latin plural of uterus, the womb, so the answer names those organs in the anatomist's form.

entries.clue: Specific tautological statement, nothing more to discuss (5,4)

blocks.note: a statement that says of one specific thing only that it is itself: that is that
the phrase that closes a matter for good

annotation.surface: A precise but circular remark that closes the conversation.
annotation.walkthrough: The first half describes the phrase itself: pointing at one specific thing and saying it is itself is a tautology. The second half is what the same phrase means when you say it.
annotation.definitionFit: Two readings of one phrase: taken literally it is a tautology, and in use it means the matter is settled and there is nothing further to be said.

entries.clue: Cynthia liberally feeds borders of herbaceous plants (9)

indicatorNotes.liberally: Letters handled liberally are handled freely, with no obligation to stay in the order they came in.
indicatorNotes.feeds: What feeds into something goes inside it, so the jumbled letters are set between the two that are left standing.
indicatorNotes.borders of: A border is an edge, so the word after it gives up its first and last letters and nothing in between.

blocks.note: the two borders of HERBACEOUS, one at each end of the answer
seven letters re-set to fill the gap between those two

annotation.surface: Cynthia generously feeding the edges of a herbaceous border.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Borders' reads as a garden bed and works as the two ends of a word, which is the whole of the misdirection. The proper name is in the clue for its seven letters and nothing else.
annotation.definitionFit: Hyacinths are the spring bulbs grown in beds and bowls for their scented spikes, so they are plants in the plainest sense of the word.

entries.clue: Out-of-line solicitor perhaps holding up Cats novel (3,6)

indicatorNotes.Out-of: Out of something is away from it, so the letter named next takes no part in what follows.
indicatorNotes.holding up: Whatever holds a thing up is underneath it, so in this down answer the piece doing the holding goes below the piece it holds.

blocks.note: a tom is a male cat, so cats in the plural are toms
a solicitor is one kind of lawyer, which 'perhaps' marks as an example
l = line, and it is the letter that goes

annotation.surface: A solicitor stepping out of line to delay a performance of Cats.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics make Cats the Lloyd Webber musical, and what the clue wants is male cats. 'Out-of-line' does two jobs at once: the line is the letter L, and it is the letter removed.
annotation.definitionFit: The Adventures of Tom Sawyer is Mark Twain's 1876 book about a boy on the Mississippi, and the answer is the name the novel goes by.

entries.clue: Dance in two circles? (5)

blocks.note: the first circle is a disc, the flat round thing records were cut on
the second is the letter O, which is a circle drawn

annotation.surface: A dance performed inside a pair of rings.
annotation.walkthrough: Two circles of different kinds, one an object and one a letter, and the question mark is the setter admitting the phrasing is loose. The little word 'in' does nothing but join.
annotation.definitionFit: A disco is an evening of dancing to records, and in British use a dance and a disco name the same event.

entries.clue: Do sad sucker, unfortunately (5,4)

indicatorNotes.unfortunately: What happens unfortunately happens badly, and letters badly placed are letters free to be set in any order.

blocks.note: nine letters waiting to be re-set

annotation.surface: Doing over a sad and gullible fool, unluckily.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Do' is the hairdresser's noun, not the verb the surface offers, and those two letters are the entire definition. The insult in the middle of the clue is the anagram fodder.
annotation.definitionFit: A duck's arse is the 1950s Teddy boy haircut, greased back so the sides meet in a ridge down the neck, and 'do' is British informal for any hairstyle.

entries.clue: Musical arrangement nowhere near interesting enough initially (5)

indicatorNotes.initially: An initial is the letter a word starts with, so each word in the run hands over only its first.

blocks.note: the opening letters of the five words in order

annotation.surface: A musical setting that is nowhere near interesting enough.
annotation.walkthrough: Five words in a row give up their first letters while the sentence reads as a verdict on a dull arrangement. 'Musical' is the noun, a show, rather than the adjective it looks like.
annotation.definitionFit: Annie is the Broadway musical about the red-haired orphan who sings 'Tomorrow', so the answer is the name of a show.

entries.clue: Hindu retreats from animals under tree (7)

indicatorNotes.under: In a down answer what is under something sits below it, so the animals go beneath the tree rather than after it.

blocks.note: the ash is a common British hedgerow tree
rams are male sheep

annotation.surface: Hindus backing away from animals standing under a tree.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Retreats' is a noun here, a place people withdraw to, though the surface hands you the verb. The Sanskrit ashrama means a stage of life as well as a hermitage.
annotation.definitionFit: An ashram is the hermitage or community where a Hindu teacher's followers live simply, withdrawn from the world.

entries.clue: Spy hints for shifting 50 tiny things (9)

indicatorNotes.shifting: Anything shifting will not stay where it was put, so those letters may be set down in a new order.

blocks.note: a mole is the spy planted inside the organisation he reports on
a cue is a hint to act on, four of the five letters to be re-set
L is the Roman fifty, the fifth letter joining that jumble

annotation.surface: A spy's tips on moving fifty small items.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Spy' is the planted kind, a mole, and the number is the Roman numeral thrown in with the letters beside it. The definition is as literal as it looks, which is rare in a clue this busy.
annotation.definitionFit: A molecule is the smallest unit a compound can be divided into and still be itself — a handful of atoms — so they are tiny things by nature.

entries.clue: Crushes young relative (7)

annotation.definitionNote: The second half only works once the letters are re-divided: read as two words they are a verb and its preposition, while the answer as one word is a noun.

blocks.note: read as one word — the boy a new husband or wife brings to a marriage
read as two words — what a boot does to a beetle, treading right on it

annotation.surface: Something that crushes a young member of the family.
annotation.walkthrough: The seven letters divide in two different places: as one word they are a family member, as two they are a foot coming down. Nothing in the clue says which division to try.
annotation.definitionFit: A stepson is the son your spouse already had, a young relative by marriage; split into two words the same letters are what you do to something underfoot.

entries.clue: What could be stuffing heroin, top-notch, inside empty holder (9)

indicatorNotes.inside: What is inside a thing sits within it, so the letters named go between the two that are left.
indicatorNotes.empty: An empty word has nothing in the middle, so only its outer letters are left standing.

blocks.note: horse is the street name for heroin
HOLDER emptied of everything between its ends leaves H and R
A1 is the shipping register's mark for first class, its figure one written here as the letter I

annotation.surface: Top-grade heroin being packed inside an empty container.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Horse' for heroin is the street name, and 'top-notch' is the old insurance grade A1 with its numeral read as a letter. The stuffing is the upholsterer's, not the smuggler's.
annotation.definitionFit: Horsehair was the traditional stuffing for mattresses and chair seats, springy and slow to rot, so it is one thing stuffing could turn out to be.

entries.clue: Dismiss defective item with missing cap (5)

indicatorNotes.missing: What is missing is not there, so the letter named beside it takes no part in the answer.

blocks.note: an item that fails inspection is a reject
the cap is the letter on top, the R at the front of REJECT

annotation.surface: Throwing out a faulty thing that has lost its lid.
annotation.walkthrough: A cap sits on top, so in a down answer it is the first letter that comes off, while the surface hands you a bottle. 'Dismiss' is the throwing-out sense rather than the waving-away one.
annotation.definitionFit: To eject somebody is to throw them out of the place they were in — the bouncer's job — which is to dismiss them from it.

entries.clue: Vacuous roommate qualifying for makeover (5)

indicatorNotes.Vacuous: Something vacuous is hollow, empty in the middle, so the word after it keeps only its two end letters.

blocks.note: ROOMMATE hollowed out leaves its R and its E
to be fit for something is to qualify for it

annotation.surface: An empty-headed flatmate who qualifies for a television makeover.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vacuous' works twice over: it insults the flatmate in the surface and hollows the word out in the parsing. 'Qualifying' is being fit for a thing, not passing an examination.
annotation.definitionFit: A refit is the overhaul a ship or a shop gets when it is stripped out and fitted again, which is a makeover in overalls.

entries.clue: Black market consumes bachelor (5)

indicatorNotes.consumes: What is consumed is swallowed whole, so the letter named goes down inside the word before it.

blocks.note: a sale is a market for goods, and the four letters open to take a letter in
b = bachelor, as in the BA and BSc degrees

annotation.surface: An illegal trade that swallows up a single man.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Black market' is one phrase in the surface and two separate jobs in the clue: the first word is the definition and the second supplies the letters it goes into.
annotation.definitionFit: Sable is the heraldic and poetic word for black, taken from the dark winter fur of the marten of that name.

entries.clue: Play both sides of early Corrs demo for a broadcast (1,6,2,6)

annotation.definitionNote: Shakespeare's title begins with 'The'; with 'a' in front the phrase is one play of that kind rather than that particular one, which is what lets the definition stand.

indicatorNotes.both sides of: The sides of a word are its two edges, so the word after it gives up its first and last letters only.
indicatorNotes.broadcast: Seed is broadcast by being flung wide across a field, so the letters are scattered and land in a new order.

blocks.note: the two sides of EARLY, its first letter and its last
thirteen more letters for the jumble, small words and all

annotation.surface: Both sides of an early Corrs demo tape going out on the radio.
annotation.walkthrough: The Corrs are the Irish family band, and 'broadcast' is the sowing sense — seed flung wide — rather than the radio one the tape sets up. Even 'for' and 'a' are fodder here.
annotation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's farce of twins mistaken for one another is a comedy of errors, so the phrase names a play as well as any farcical muddle.

entries.clue: Legislator in defence association cutting first half of speech (7)

indicatorNotes.cutting: Something cutting into a thing goes right through the middle of it, so the letters named are set inside the ones before them.

blocks.note: a sermon is a speech, and the first three of its six letters are SER
NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation, has been the West's defence alliance since 1949

annotation.surface: A lawmaker inside a defence alliance who cuts a speech short.
annotation.walkthrough: The speech is a sermon, and 'first half' is exactly three letters of its six. The definition is the opening word, with 'in' joining it to the rest and contributing nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: A senator sits in the upper house that makes a country's laws, in Washington or in ancient Rome, so legislating is the job itself.

entries.clue: Crime from boy after beverage round back of bar (7)

indicatorNotes.after: In an across answer what comes after something follows it, so the boy's letters end up at the back rather than the front.
indicatorNotes.round: What goes round a thing encloses it, so the drink's letters part to take the single letter inside.

blocks.note: tea is the beverage, and its three letters open after the first
the back of BAR is its last letter
a son is somebody's boy

annotation.surface: A boy wanting a drink round the back of the bar.
annotation.walkthrough: The drink is tea, where a crossword's beverage nearly always lands, and 'bar' gives up nothing but its final letter. The boy is the standard three-letter son.
annotation.definitionFit: Treason is the crime of betraying your own country or its sovereign, the one offence the law still calls high.
